```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Synthetic teaching data for BIOS 6301. Not real patients.
set.seed(6301)
n <- 60
trial <- data.frame(
  id        = sprintf("P%03d", 1:n),
  arm       = rep(c("Placebo", "Treatment"), each = n / 2),
  site      = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  age       = round(rnorm(n, 61, 9)),
  sex       = sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE),
  weight_kg = round(rnorm(n, 82, 15), 1),
  sbp_0     = round(rnorm(n, 148, 14)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trial$sbp_12 <- round(trial$sbp_0 -
  ifelse(trial$arm == "Treatment", rnorm(n, 14, 8), rnorm(n, 3, 8)))

# Added for this session only, and nothing else is changed:
#   sbp_6  - a middle visit, so a ribbon has somewhere to run
#   crp    - a deliberately right-skewed lab value, for the log-scale slide
#   site_f - site as a labelled factor, so facet strips read as words
trial$sbp_6 <- round(trial$sbp_0 -
  ifelse(trial$arm == "Treatment", rnorm(n, 8, 7), rnorm(n, 2, 7)))
trial$crp    <- round(exp(rnorm(n, 1.1, 0.9)), 2)
trial$site_f <- factor(trial$site, levels = 1:4,
                       labels = paste("Site", 1:4))

# One row per patient-visit, using the reshape from Session 7.
trial_long <- trial |>
  select(id, arm, sbp_0, sbp_6, sbp_12) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(starts_with("sbp_"),
                      names_to = "week", names_prefix = "sbp_",
                      values_to = "sbp") |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week))
arm_col <- c(Placebo = "#D55E00", Treatment = "#0072B2")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))

# Every figure fills the width of its container; fig-width and fig-height then
# control the aspect ratio and the text size relative to the panel.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(out.width = "100%")
```

# 1 · Base R graphics {.section-divider}


## The teaching data

All observations in this session are **synthetic**.

```{r}
#| label: base-data-preview
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(head(trial[c("id", "arm", "age", "sbp_0", "sbp_12")], 4))
```

- One row represents one participant.
- `sbp_0` and `sbp_12` are systolic blood pressure at baseline and week 12, in mmHg.
- `trial_long` has one row per participant per visit, as in Session 7.


## A plot starts with a question

| Question | Useful starting plot |
|---|---|
| What values and unusual observations occur? | Histogram or dot plot |
| How do participant values differ by arm? | Boxplot with individual points |
| How does baseline relate to follow-up? | Scatterplot |
| How does one participant change over time? | Connected points, grouped by ID |
| How many participants come from each site? | Bar chart of counts |

The same plotting function may answer different questions. Labels and the
observation unit tell the reader which question you mean.

## A labelled scatterplot in base R

```{r}
#| label: base-scatter-labelled
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12,
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
     ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
     main = "Baseline and follow-up",
     pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
```

`plot(x, y)` puts the first numeric vector on x and the second on y.


## Common base R plotting arguments

| Argument | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `pch` | Point symbol | `pch = 19` for a filled circle |
| `col` | Colour | `col = "steelblue"` |
| `cex` | Symbol/text size multiplier | `cex = 1.3` |
| `lty`, `lwd` | Line pattern and width | `lty = 2, lwd = 2` |
| `xlab`, `ylab`, `main` | Axis labels and title | `ylab = "SBP (mmHg)"` |
| `xlim`, `ylim` | Display limits | `ylim = c(90, 190)` |

Use `?plot.default` and `?par` to look up options as needed.

## Which participant has lower follow-up SBP? {#question-identity .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

The scatterplot has **baseline SBP on x** and **week-12 SBP on y**.

Imagine a line where **y = x**.

**A.** A point above the line

**B.** A point below the line

**C.** A point on the line

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**B.** Below the line, week-12 SBP is lower than baseline.

On the line, the two measurements are equal.
:::


## Adding a reference line

```{r}
#| label: base-identity
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12,
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)",
     xlim = c(90, 190), ylim = c(90, 190), pch = 19)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

`a` is the intercept and `b` is the slope. Below the line, follow-up is lower
than baseline. This line represents equality, not a fitted regression.

## Colours and a legend by treatment arm

```{r}
#| label: base-arm-legend
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12, pch = 19,
     col = arm_col[trial$arm],
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
legend("topleft", legend = names(arm_col),
       col = arm_col, pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

`arm_col` is a named vector: `c(Placebo = "#D55E00", Treatment = "#0072B2")`.
Indexing it by arm assigns the same colour consistently.


## New plot or added marks?

| Creates a new plot | Adds to the current plot |
|---|---|
| `plot()` | `points()` |
| `hist()` | `lines()` |
| `boxplot()` | `abline()` |
| `barplot()` | `text()`, `legend()` |

For example, `points(x, y, col = "red")` adds observations to existing axes.
Calling `plot(x, y)` again normally starts a new plot.


## Connected measurements from one participant

```{r}
#| label: base-trajectory
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
weeks <- c(0, 6, 12)
values <- c(trial$sbp_0[1], trial$sbp_6[1], trial$sbp_12[1])
plot(weeks, values, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Week", ylab = "SBP (mmHg)", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = weeks)
```

`type = "p"` draws points, `"l"` draws lines, and `"b"` draws both.
Base R connects points in supplied order, so arrange time first.

## Histogram bins change the picture

```{r}
#| label: base-breaks
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$sbp_0, breaks = seq(80, 210, 5),
     main = "5-mmHg bins", xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)")
hist(trial$sbp_0, breaks = seq(80, 220, 20),
     main = "20-mmHg bins", xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)")
par(saved_par)
```

A vector in `breaks` specifies bin boundaries. A single number requests an
approximate number of bins. A pattern should not depend on one convenient choice.

## Different bins, different participants? {#question-bins .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN COMPARE]{.question-time}

The previous slide showed the same baseline SBP values in **5-mmHg** and **20-mmHg** bins.

**Did the participants change, or did the grouping of values change?**

Tell your neighbor one pattern that could look different.

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
The observations stayed the same. Only the bin boundaries changed.

Apparent peaks and gaps can change. Check more than one reasonable bin width.
:::


## Boxplots with participant-level values

```{r}
#| label: base-stripchart
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, outline = FALSE,
        ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)", xlab = "")
stripchart(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial,
           vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 19, col = "steelblue", add = TRUE)
```

- `outline = FALSE` hides the boxplot's **outlier symbols**. Box borders and whiskers remain.
- `stripchart()` then draws **all observations**, including values beyond the whiskers.
- Together, these calls show each observation once, without duplicate outlier symbols.


## Bar charts use counts or summaries

```{r}
#| label: base-bar-counts
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
site_counts <- table(trial$site_f)
barplot(site_counts, col = "steelblue",
        xlab = "Recruiting site", ylab = "Number of participants")
```

`table()` calculates the counts. `barplot()` draws their heights.
A histogram instead bins a numeric variable such as blood pressure.

## Optional: two distribution diagnostics {#base-diagnostics}

| Plot | What it shows | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| **Empirical CDF (ECDF)** | The observed cumulative distribution | At a given SBP, read the proportion of participants at or below it |
| **Normal Q–Q plot** | Sample quantiles against theoretical normal quantiles | Points near a straight line suggest an approximately normal distribution |

- The ECDF uses **every observation**, with no histogram bins.
- In a normal Q–Q plot, systematic curvature or tail departures suggest departures from normality.


## Optional: ECDF and normal Q–Q examples {#base-diagnostics-example}

```{r}
#| label: base-ecdf-qq
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(ecdf(trial$sbp_0), main = "Cumulative proportion",
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Proportion at or below x")
qqnorm(trial$sbp_0, main = "Normal Q-Q plot")
qqline(trial$sbp_0, col = "steelblue")
par(saved_par)
```

**Left:** proportion at or below each SBP value. **Right:** sample versus normal quantiles.

A roughly straight Q–Q pattern **supports approximate normality**. This is a visual assessment, without a p-value.


## Multiple panels and graphics state

```r
saved_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # one row, two columns
hist(trial$sbp_0)
hist(trial$sbp_12)
par(saved_par)                    # restore changed settings
```

- `par()` affects the current graphics device.
- Restore settings after the multi-panel display.
- If separate panels need direct comparison, choose common axis limits.
- `par(mfrow = c(1, 1))` resets the layout, but does not reset every other option.

## Raster and vector figures {#raster-vector}

| | PNG: raster image | PDF: vector graphics |
|---|---|---|
| Stores | A grid of coloured pixels | Drawing instructions for lines, shapes, and text |
| When enlarged | Individual pixels can become visible | Vector elements remain sharp as they scale |
| Size settings | Width, height, and pixel density | Physical page width and height |

**A PDF has no single overall DPI for its vector elements.**

A PDF can also contain raster images. Those images retain their pixel-resolution limits.


## Resolution: pixels and physical size {#resolution-dpi}

**DPI** means dots per inch. For raster export, R uses this setting as **pixels per inch (PPI)**.

**Pixel width = width in inches × DPI**

| A 6 × 4 inch PNG | Pixel dimensions |
|---|---|
| 150 DPI | 900 × 600 pixels |
| 300 DPI | 1800 × 1200 pixels |
| 600 DPI | 3600 × 2400 pixels |

At fixed physical size, higher DPI creates more pixels. At fixed pixel dimensions, changing DPI changes the physical size, without adding detail.


## Saving a base R figure

```r
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
png("output/base-sbp.png", width = 6, height = 4,
    units = "in", res = 300)
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12,
     xlab = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", ylab = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
dev.off()
```

The file device receives drawing commands until `dev.off()` closes it.
This PNG has **1800 × 1200 pixels**: 6 × 4 inches at `res = 300`.

For a 6 × 4 inch vector PDF, open `pdf("output/base-sbp.pdf", width = 6, height = 4)` instead. **No `res` or `dpi` argument.**


## Base graphics in four functions {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: base-four
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$sbp_0, main = "hist", xlab = "SBP baseline")
boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, main = "boxplot", xlab = "")
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12, main = "plot", xlab = "Week 0",
     ylab = "Week 12")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.smaller}
`par(mfrow = c(1, 3))` splits the device into a 1 × 3 grid. It is **device
state**: it stays set until you change it back.
:::


## A quick panel of distributions {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: base-diagnostic
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.5
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$age,       main = "age")
hist(trial$weight_kg, main = "weight_kg")
hist(trial$sbp_0,     main = "sbp_0")
hist(trial$crp,       main = "crp")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Four columns, one screen, five seconds. You are not making a figure — you are
**checking that the file is what you think it is**. `crp` is right-skewed and
you now know it before you fit anything.
:::


## Two plotting workflows

- **Base graphics:** draw to a graphics device, then add points, lines, or labels.
  Many functions share options such as `col`, `xlab`, and `ylim`.
- **ggplot2:** build a plot object, then add or change layers and scales.
  Grouping, legends, and facets follow shared rules.
- Both can produce reproducible, publication-quality figures. Choose the
  workflow that makes your analysis easy to understand and maintain.


# 2 · Building a first ggplot {.section-divider}

## Our ggplot2 route {.concept}

We will keep returning to the same synthetic blood-pressure study.

1. **Build a plot:** baseline versus follow-up.
2. **Choose displays:** distributions and arm comparisons.
3. **Add summaries:** means, intervals, and fitted trends.
4. **Show repeated visits:** one line per participant.
5. **Refine and export:** scales, labels, accessibility, and file size.




## A plot is a specification {.concept}

**Question:** How does baseline blood pressure relate to week 12?

- **Data:** one row per participant.
- **x:** baseline SBP.
- **y:** week 12 SBP.
- **Marks:** one point per participant.

```r
ggplot(trial, aes(x = sbp_0, y = sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()
```

We describe the data and its visual mappings, then choose how to draw it.


## Seven components, plus a theme {.concept}

The first four determine the data shown in a layer.

| Component | In our study |
|---|---|
| **Data** | Participant records in `trial` |
| **Aesthetics** | `aes(x = sbp_0, y = sbp_12)` |
| **Geom** | `geom_point()` draws each participant |
| **Stat** | Points use raw values; a histogram counts bins |

Most early examples need only data, mappings, and a geom.

## Scales, coordinates, facets, and theme {.concept}

The remaining components control how the plot appears.

| Component | Role | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Scales** | Translate values to positions or colours | Logarithmic y axis |
| **Coordinates** | Define the plotting space and view | Zoom into a region |
| **Facets** | Repeat a plot for subsets | One panel per site |
| **Theme** | Style non-data elements | Fonts and grid lines |

We will add these after the basic plot answers the scientific question.

## What will this code draw? {#question-empty .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

```r
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12))
```

**A.** A scatterplot with participant points

**B.** Axes without participant points

**C.** An error

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**B.** Data and mappings establish the axes.

Adding `geom_point()` draws the participant marks.
:::


## A first ggplot: axes, then points {.concept}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: mvp
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.9
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12))
```
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: mvp-plus
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.9
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::
:::

Data and mappings establish the axes. The geom adds visible marks.



## The pipe and the plus sign have different jobs

```r
trial |>
  filter(site == 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
       y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
```

- `|>` passes the filtered data into `ggplot()`.
- `+` adds plotting components to the ggplot object.
- Put `+` at the end of a line when continuing the expression.
- `ggplot(...) |> geom_point()` does not mean “add a point layer.”

## A ggplot object can be revised

```{r}
#| label: gg-object
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
p_scatter <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()
p_scatter + labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)",
                 y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
```

`p_scatter + ...` displays a revised plot. To keep that version, assign it:
`p_scatter <- p_scatter + labs(...)`.

## Will these points be blue? {#question-color .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

```r
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))
```

**A.** Yes, because the code says “blue”

**B.** It maps a category named “blue”

**C.** It cannot run

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**B.** Inside `aes()`, “blue” becomes a category mapped through a colour scale.

For fixed blue points: `geom_point(colour = "blue")`.
:::


## `aes()` means *map*. Outside means *set* {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: aes-inside
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
                  colour = arm)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: aes-outside
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue")
```
:::
:::

::: {.smaller}
Inside `aes()`: colour **carries information**, and you get a legend.
Outside: colour is fixed, and this setting does not create a mapped legend.
:::


## Colour, fill, and shape

```{r}
#| label: gg-fill-colour
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12, fill = arm)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, colour = "black", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arm_col) +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
```

For shapes 21–25, `fill` controls the interior and `colour` controls the border.
For most other point shapes, use `colour`. For bars, `fill` colours the interior.

# 3 · Choosing a display {.section-divider}

## Questions that need different displays {.concept}

- **Distribution:** What baseline values occur?
- **Comparison:** How do week-12 values differ between arms?
- **Counts:** How many participants belong to each category?

We will keep the study data, but change the variables and marks.

## Choosing a geom

A **geom** is a layer's drawing method: points, lines, bars, text, or another mark.
Some geoms also compute a default summary before drawing.

| Your data/question | Start with |
|---|---|
| Two numeric measurements per person | `geom_point()` |
| One numeric variable's distribution | `geom_histogram()` |
| A numeric outcome across groups | `geom_boxplot()` plus points |
| Counts of records by category | `geom_bar()` |
| Heights already calculated in a table | `geom_col()` |
| Repeated measurements within a person | `geom_line()` with `group = id` |

## Optional: complete ggplot2 geom catalogue {#geom-catalogue}

The next slides list the exported `geom_*()` functions in the ggplot2 version
used to render this deck, including aliases and older interfaces.

- They are a **lookup reference**, not a memorization requirement.
- Extension-package geoms, such as `ggrepel::geom_text_repel()`, are separate.
- `stat_*()`, scales, and themes are different function families.

[Skip the catalogue and continue to distributions](#core-distributions)

[Official ggplot2 function reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html)

```{r}
    geom_bin_2d = "Counts in rectangular x/y bins",
    geom_hex = "Counts in hexagonal x/y bins",
    geom_density_2d = "Contours of an estimated x/y density",
    geom_density_2d_filled = "Filled regions of an estimated x/y density",
    geom_contour = "Contour lines for supplied grid values z",
    geom_contour_filled = "Filled contour regions for supplied grid values z"),
  maps = c(
    geom_polygon = "Closed shapes from ordered vertices",
    geom_map = "Values joined to a separate map polygon table",
    geom_sf = "Geometry from an sf spatial object",
    geom_sf_text = "Text located using sf geometry",
    geom_sf_label = "Boxed text located using sf geometry"),
  aliases = c(
    geom_bin2d = "Alias of geom_bin_2d",
    geom_density2d = "Alias of geom_density_2d",
    geom_density2d_filled = "Alias of geom_density_2d_filled")
)
exported_geoms <- sort(getNamespaceExports("ggplot2"))
exported_geoms <- exported_geoms[startsWith(exported_geoms, "geom_")]
listed_geoms <- unlist(lapply(geom_catalogue, names), use.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(listed_geoms), setequal(exported_geoms, listed_geoms))
show_geoms <- function(group) {
  entries <- geom_catalogue[[group]]
  knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Function = paste0("`", names(entries), "()`"),
    Purpose = unname(entries)
  ), row.names = FALSE)
}
gallery_pair <- function(left, right) {
  grid::grid.newpage()
  print(left + theme_minimal(base_size = 15),
        vp = grid::viewport(x = 0.25, width = 0.48))
  print(right + theme_minimal(base_size = 15),
        vp = grid::viewport(x = 0.75, width = 0.48))
}
gallery_summary <- trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(m = mean(sbp_12), se = sd(sbp_12) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")
gallery_time <- trial_long |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarise(m = mean(sbp), se = sd(sbp) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")
```

## Geom reference: points and labels {.geom-reference}

```{r}
show_geoms("points")
```

## Geom examples: points and jitter {.gallery}

```{r}

#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
gallery_pair(
  ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
    geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col, guide = "none") +
    labs(title = "geom_point()", x = "Baseline SBP", y = "Week 12 SBP"),
  ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col, guide = "none") +
    labs(title = "geom_jitter()", x = NULL, y = "Week 12 SBP")
)
```

Points show a relationship between two measurements. Jitter separates
overlapping observations within categories. Both show individual participants.

## Geom reference: connected observations {.geom-reference}

```{r}

show_geoms("paths")
```

Connecting observations implies a relationship or order. It is usually
inappropriate to connect unrelated participants just because their rows are adjacent.

## Geom examples: line and step {.gallery}

```{r}
#| label: gallery-lines
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
gallery_pair(
  ggplot(gallery_time, aes(week, m, colour = arm)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
    labs(title = "geom_line()", x = "Week", y = "Mean SBP"),
  ggplot(data.frame(day = c(0, 2, 5, 8), dose = c(0, 10, 20, 10)),
         aes(day, dose)) +
    geom_step(linewidth = 1, colour = "#0072B2") +
    labs(title = "geom_step()", x = "Day", y = "Dose (mg)")
)
```

A line connects measured summaries. A step can represent a dose held constant
until the next change. The right-hand schedule is a separate synthetic example.

## Geom reference: intervals {.geom-reference}

```{r}

```

For new horizontal error bars, use `geom_errorbar(orientation = "y")`
with `xmin` and `xmax`. The plotting function does not determine whether your
interval means SD, SE, or a confidence interval.

## Geom examples: two ways to draw an interval {.gallery}

```{r}
#| label: gallery-intervals
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
interval_plot <- ggplot(gallery_summary,
  aes(arm, m, ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean week 12 SBP")
gallery_pair(
  interval_plot + geom_pointrange(colour = "#0072B2") +
    labs(title = "geom_pointrange()"),
  interval_plot + geom_errorbar(width = 0.15, colour = "#0072B2") +
    geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#0072B2") +
    labs(title = "geom_errorbar() + geom_point()")
)
```

These show the same means and approximate 95% confidence intervals.
Pointrange draws both marks; errorbar supplies the interval with end caps.

## Geom examples: binned counts and contours {.gallery}

```{r}
#| label: gallery-surfaces
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
surface_grid <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(nrow(volcano)),
                            y = seq_len(ncol(volcano)))
surface_grid$z <- as.vector(volcano)

  ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +

         fill = "Count"),
  ggplot(surface_grid, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
```

## Geom example: regions defined by vertices {.gallery}

```{r}
#| label: gallery-polygons
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9

regions <- data.frame(

)
ggplot(regions, aes(x, y, group = region, fill = region)) +
```


This deck lists **`r length(exported_geoms)` exported names**, including aliases,
for **ggplot2 `r as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2"))`**.

Use `?geom_point` or the
[official reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html) for arguments.

## Back to the study: distributions {#core-distributions .concept}

The catalogue shows the range of available marks. Now we use a small set to
answer the study questions.

**First question:** What is the distribution of baseline SBP?

Compare a histogram's bins with a density curve's smoothing.


## Distributions: histogram and density {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: geom-hist
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 8,
                 fill = "grey35")
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: geom-density
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0)) +
  geom_density(fill = "grey80")
```
:::
:::

::: {.smaller}
`binwidth = 8` uses 8-mmHg bins. `bins = 30` asks for a number of bins.
Either choice needs checking: try alternatives and see whether the pattern persists.

**The base R way:** `hist(trial$sbp_0)` · `plot(density(trial$sbp_0))`
:::


## Distributions compared: boxplot and violin {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: geom-box
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: geom-violin
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey85")
```
:::
:::

::: {.smaller}
A boxplot shows the median, quartiles, whiskers, and possible outlying points.
A violin shows an estimated density. Neither displays the sample size by default.

**The base R way:** `boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial)`
:::


## Show the data, not only the summary {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: geom-jitter
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.9
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.45, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.7, size = 2)
```

::: {.smaller}
`outlier.shape = NA` stops the boxplot drawing outliers that `geom_jitter()`
already drew. Two marks for one observation is a real error, not a style choice.
:::


## Sixty participants, fewer visible dots? {#question-overlap .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

Our scatterplot contains **60 participants**.

Could it show fewer than 60 separately visible dots?

**A.** Yes, observations can overlap

**B.** No, R always separates the points

**C.** Only if some participants were removed

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**A.** Multiple observations can occupy the same or nearby plotting positions.

Transparency or suitable jitter can help reveal overlap.
:::


## Overlap can hide observations

```{r}
#| label: gg-reproducible-jitter
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12,
                                        height = 0, seed = 6301),
             alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Week 12 SBP (mmHg)")
```

Horizontal jitter separates tied marks. `height = 0` preserves the measured
outcome, and `seed` makes the offsets repeatable. Alpha reduces visual overlap.

## Counts versus a precomputed table

```{r}
#| label: gg-count-table
#| echo: false
counts <- trial |> count(arm)
knitr::kable(counts)
```

```r
# One row per participant: let the geom count
ggplot(trial, aes(arm)) + geom_bar()

# One row per arm: heights are already calculated
ggplot(counts, aes(arm, n)) + geom_col()
```

Both give the same counts here. A mean or percentage already stored in `y`
usually calls for `geom_col()`, not the default `geom_bar()` statistic.

## Comparisons: bars, and position adjustments {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: geom-bar
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.7
ggplot(trial, aes(site_f, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

::: {.smaller}
| `position =` | Shows | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `"stack"` *(default)* | Counts, one bar per group | Totals |
| `"dodge"` | Counts, side by side | Comparing subgroups |
| `"fill"` | Proportions, all bars to 1 | Composition — but hides n |
:::


# 4 · Adding summaries and uncertainty {.section-divider}

## Participant values and group summaries {.concept}

**Question:** What is the average week-12 SBP in each arm, and how uncertain is it?

1. Keep the participant-level data visible.
2. Calculate an arm-level summary table.
3. Draw a summary layer from that table.
4. State what its interval means.

The raw data and summary layers have different observation units.


## What do these error bars tell us? {#question-intervals .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

A caption says: **“Mean week-12 SBP with a 95% confidence interval for each arm mean.”**

**A.** The interval contains 95% of participant SBP values

**B.** It describes uncertainty about each arm’s population mean

**C.** It shows the minimum and maximum SBP

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**B.** A confidence interval for a mean concerns that population mean.

The individual points show participant-level variation.
:::


## What do the intervals mean?

| Interval | Describes |
|---|---|
| Mean ± SD | Spread of individual measurements around their mean |
| Mean ± SE | Estimated sampling variability of the mean |
| Confidence interval | Uncertainty about a population parameter under a model |
| Prediction interval | Uncertainty about a new individual observation |

The same `geom_errorbar()` can draw any of these. Its inputs do not tell the
reader which one you intended. State the meaning and method in the caption.

The earlier `mean ± 1.96 * SE` examples use an approximate 95% confidence interval.
The longitudinal ribbon gives intervals at each visit, not a model of change.

## Uncertainty: an estimate needs an interval {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: geom-pointrange
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.6
by_arm <- trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12),
            se = sd(sbp_12) / sqrt(n()))

ggplot(by_arm, aes(arm, mean_sbp)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
                      ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se))
```


## A layer can use its own data

```{r}
#| label: gg-separate-data
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0,
                                        seed = 6301), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = by_arm, aes(x = arm, y = mean_sbp),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 5,
             colour = "#0072B2")
```

Grey points use participant data. Blue diamonds use the summary table.
`inherit.aes = FALSE` makes the summary layer use only its own mappings.

## Relationships: points and a smooth {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: geom-smooth
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(trial, aes(age, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, alpha = 0.15)
```

::: {.smaller}
`method = "lm"` specifies a linear fit. With `method = NULL`, ggplot2 chooses
loess or GAM according to the largest group's size. The band describes
uncertainty in the fitted mean, not a prediction interval for an individual.
:::


## Layer-specific mappings

```{r}
#| label: gg-layer-mapping
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = arm)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col)
```

Colour belongs only to the points here. The smooth uses all participants
together. Putting `colour = arm` in the global `aes()` would fit one line per arm.


# 5 · Showing repeated visits {.section-divider}

## A new question needs a different data shape {.concept}

**Question:** How does blood pressure change over the three visits?

- One row in `trial`: one participant, with visits in separate columns.
- One row in `trial_long`: one participant at one visit.
- Individual lines need `id`, `week`, and `sbp`.
- Group-average lines need an arm-by-week summary.

Session 7's wide-to-long reshape makes these plots easier to specify.


## Did reshaping triple our study? {#question-visits .lecture-question}

[75 SECONDS · THINK, THEN COMPARE]{.question-time}

There are **60 participants** and **three visits per participant**: weeks 0, 6, and 12.

After reshaping to long form:

1. How many rows do we have?
2. How many participants do we have?
3. Which variable keeps each person’s line together?

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**180 rows, 60 participants, and `group = id` for individual trajectories.**

One long-table row represents one participant at one visit.
:::


## Plotting repeated visits uses the long table

```r
trial_long <- trial |>
  select(id, arm, sbp_0, sbp_6, sbp_12) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(starts_with("sbp_"),
                     names_to = "week", names_prefix = "sbp_",
                     values_to = "sbp") |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week))
```

```{r}
#| label: gg-long-preview
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(head(trial_long, 3))
```

The first participant contributes three rows. Their shared `id` tells the
plot which measurements belong together.

## One line per participant

```{r}
#| label: gg-trajectories
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(trial_long, aes(week, sbp, group = id, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col, guide = "none")
```

`colour = arm` alone would define only two colour groups. `group = id` tells
the line layer to connect each person's own measurements.

## Optional: line versus path {#line-path-reference}

```{r}
#| label: gg-line-path
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
route <- data.frame(x = c(1, 3, 2), y = c(1, 2, 3))
routes <- rbind(transform(route, display = "geom_line"),
                transform(route, display = "geom_path"))
ggplot(routes, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = subset(routes, display == "geom_line")) +
  geom_path(data = subset(routes, display == "geom_path")) +
  facet_wrap(~ display)
```

`geom_line()` sorts by x within each group. `geom_path()` follows row order,
which is useful for an ordered route through space.

## Uncertainty over time: the ribbon {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: geom-ribbon
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.4
by_week <- trial_long |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarise(m = mean(sbp), se = sd(sbp) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, colour = arm, fill = arm)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se),
              alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12))
```


## Facets: the same plot, split {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: facet-wrap
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ site_f, nrow = 1)
```

::: {.smaller}
`facet_wrap(~ x)` wraps one variable into panels · `facet_grid(a ~ b)` makes a
matrix of two · `scales = "free_y"` lets each panel set its own axis, **which
breaks comparability**.
:::


# 6 · Refining the display {.section-divider}

## Display choices after the plot works {.concept}

Our plot already answers a question. Now consider how readers will interpret it.

- Would a transformation make a skewed variable easier to see?
- Do we want to zoom, or intentionally exclude data?
- Can the reader identify groups and understand the labels?
- Will the exported figure remain readable at its final size?


## Scales: where the transformation belongs {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: scale-raw
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, crp)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: scale-log
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, crp)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  scale_y_log10()
```
:::
:::

::: {.smaller}
`scale_y_log10()` transforms the **scale** and keeps the axis in original units.
`aes(y = log10(crp))` transforms the **data** and labels the axis `log10(crp)`.
Prefer the scale.
:::



## Will these give the same boxplot? {#question-zoom .lecture-question}

[75 SECONDS · PREDICT, THEN DISCUSS]{.question-time}

```r
p <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot()

# A
p + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(120, 160))

# B
p + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(120, 160))
```

**Which keeps all observations in the boxplot calculation?**

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**A.** Coordinate zoom keeps the data used to calculate the boxplot.

In B, out-of-range values become missing before the calculation, so the summary can change.
:::


## Zooming versus removing observations

```r
p <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot()

p + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(120, 160))  # zoom after calculation
p + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(120, 160))
# Out-of-range values become NA before the boxplot calculation
```

- Zooming retains the full data in the statistical calculation.
- Scale limits can change quartiles, smooths, and other calculated summaries.
- If exclusion is intentional, filter the data explicitly and explain why.

## Optional: a small heatmap {#heatmap-reference}

```{r}
#| label: gg-heatmap
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
site_summary <- trial |>
  group_by(site_f, arm) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(site_summary, aes(arm, site_f, fill = mean_sbp)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Mean SBP\n(mmHg)")
```

Each cell represents a site/arm summary. Heatmaps show patterns across many
combinations; a dot plot is easier for precise comparisons of a few estimates.

## A debugging checklist for plots

| Symptom | First check |
|---|---|
| Unexpected colour legend | Did a constant go inside `aes()`? |
| One line connects different people | Is `group = id` specified? |
| Bar heights are unexpected | Does the geom count rows or use supplied y? |
| “Removed rows” warning | Missing values or scale limits? |
| Labels or layers disappear | Axis limits, layer data, and inherited mappings |
| Plot does not appear after assignment | Print the saved plot object: `p` |

Read the warning and inspect the relevant data before using `na.rm = TRUE`
to suppress a message.

# 7 · Critiquing and improving a figure {.section-divider}


## The perceptual hierarchy {.concept}

How accurately a reader can decode a quantity, best first:

| Rank | Channel | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Position** on a common scale | The number that carries your argument |
| 2 | **Length** | Second choice; needs a zero baseline |
| 3 | Angle, slope | Trends, reluctantly |
| 4 | **Area** | Rough magnitude only |
| 5 | Colour intensity, saturation | Broad patterns or a third variable |

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
For precise comparisons, prefer positions on a shared axis. Colour remains
useful for group identity and for patterns across large matrices.
:::


## Critique: what is wrong here? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: bad-figure
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
ggplot(by_arm, aes(arm, mean_sbp, fill = arm)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(128, 146)) +
  labs(title = "SBP results", x = "Group", y = "SBP") +
  theme_grey(base_size = 14)
```

::: {.smaller}
**Think for 20 seconds. Compare with a neighbor for 30 seconds.**

Name one specific choice and the mistaken impression it could create.
:::


## The same data, honestly {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: good-figure
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8,
              colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = by_arm,
    aes(y = mean_sbp,
        ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
        ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se),
    colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.9, size = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Systolic BP at 12 weeks (mmHg)",
       title = "SBP at 12 weeks by arm, with mean and 95% CI",
       subtitle = "n = 30 per arm; grey points are individual patients") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```


## Pie charts and dual axes need care {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r}
#| label: bad-pie
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 2.7
ggplot(trial, aes(x = "", fill = site_f)) +
  geom_bar(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  labs(fill = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.smaller}
**Pie charts** ask the reader to compare **angles and areas** — ranks 3 and 4.
Rank the four sites from that. Now imagine a bar chart.

**Dual axes** are worse, because the reader cannot check them:

```r
# do not
p + scale_y_continuous(
  sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * 3.2, name = "CRP")
)
```

The crossing point is set by *your* choice of scaling. Two facets, or two
panels, say the same thing without the implied claim.
:::
:::
:::


## What survives a grayscale printout? {#question-accessibility .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

A scatterplot identifies the two treatment arms using **colour alone**.

If those colours become indistinguishable, what could preserve the group information?

**A.** A larger title

**B.** Different point shapes or separate labelled panels

**C.** Thicker grid lines

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**B.** Shape or labelled panels provide another way to identify the arms.

A suitable palette helps; the group meaning should also survive without colour.
:::


## Colour-blind-safe, on purpose {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: pal-okabe
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 1.15
ok <- data.frame(x = 1:8,
                 hex = unname(palette.colors(8, "Okabe-Ito")))
ggplot(ok, aes(x, 1, fill = hex)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(title = "Okabe-Ito (categorical)") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: pal-viridis
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 1.15
ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:8), aes(x, 1, fill = factor(x))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "viridis (ordered / continuous)") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11)
```
:::
:::

::: {.smaller}
```r
# categorical - built in to R since 4.0
palette.colors(8, "Okabe-Ito")
#> #000000 #E69F00 #56B4E9 #009E73 #F0E442 #0072B2 #D55E00 #CC79A7
scale_colour_manual(values = palette.colors(3, "Okabe-Ito"))

# ordered or continuous - built in to ggplot2
scale_colour_viridis_d()   # discrete
scale_fill_viridis_c()     # continuous
```

Then print it in greyscale. If the groups stop being distinguishable, colour
was doing work that shape or a direct label should have been doing.
:::


## Label the thing, not the legend {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: direct-label
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 3.1
ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = filter(by_week, week == 12),
            aes(x = 12.4, label = arm),
            hjust = 0, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_col) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12),
                     limits = c(0, 16)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.smaller}
A legend makes the reader look away, decode, and look back — for every series.
A label next to the line costs them nothing.
:::


## Ink that is not information {.smaller}

Every mark on a figure is either **carrying information** or **competing with
it**.

::: {style="font-size:0.88em"}
| Remove | Because |
|---|---|
| Heavy grid lines, panel background | They are as visually loud as the data |
| A legend that repeats the x axis | Zero information |
| A third dimension on a 2-D quantity | Distorts area and hides marks |
| Decorative colour | Spends the strongest labelling channel on nothing |
| Gridlines on a categorical axis | There is nothing to read off |

:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
`theme_minimal()` gets you most of the way for free. The rest is deletion, and
the test is: **remove it. Did the figure lose anything?**
:::


# 8 · Exporting the final figure {.section-divider}


## Finish it: `labs()` and a theme {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: publication
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.5
p_final <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.45, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(data = by_arm,
                  aes(y = mean_sbp,
                      ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
                      ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se),
                  colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SBP at 12 weeks (mmHg)",
       caption = "Mean and 95% CI. n = 30 per arm.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
p_final
```


## Same code, different-sized figures? {#question-export .lecture-question}

[60 SECONDS · THINK, THEN VOTE]{.question-time}

Two collaborators run:

```r
ggsave("figure.png", plot = p_final)
```

Their RStudio plot panes have different dimensions.

**Could the saved figures have different dimensions too?**

::: {.fragment .question-answer}
**Yes.** Without explicit width and height, the export can use the current graphics device’s size.

Specify `width`, `height`, and `units`; choose DPI for a raster export.
:::


## `ggsave()`, with the arguments filled in {.smaller}

```r
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "output/fig-sbp-arm.png",
  plot     = p_final,
  width    = 6.5,     # inches - the column width of your journal
  height   = 4, units = "in",
  dpi      = 300,     # pixels per inch for this raster PNG
  bg       = "white"
)
```

::: {.smaller}
| Argument | Leave it out and you get |
|---|---|
| `width`, `height` | The last size of your **plot pane**. Irreproducible by construction |
| `dpi` | PNG pixel density defaults to 300; it does not set vector PDF sharpness |
| `bg` | Background comes from the plot theme and may be transparent |
| `.pdf` / `.svg` extension | Vector marks scale without pixelation; embedded raster layers still have finite resolution |
:::


## PNG versus PDF with `ggsave()` {#ggsave-png-pdf}

```r
# Raster: 6 x 4 inches at 300 DPI = 1800 x 1200 pixels
ggsave("output/figure.png", plot = p_final,
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# Vector: 6 x 4 inch page; no raster DPI is needed
ggsave("output/figure.pdf", plot = p_final,
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")
```

For PDF at a fixed size in inches, changing `dpi` does **not** sharpen vector lines or text.

With `units = "px"`, `ggsave()` uses `dpi` to convert pixel dimensions to physical size, even for PDF. Prefer inches or cm for vector exports.


## Why the plot pane is not a workflow {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Export → paste

Right-click, copy, paste into Word.

**Nothing records what produced it.** The data changes, the figure does not, and
no warning appears anywhere.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### `ggsave()` in the document

The figure is regenerated when its code executes during rendering.

The script records the data and plotting steps. Check data versions and caching
settings so the figure stays aligned with the analysis.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
A pasted figure is the same class of error as a number typed by hand — and it is
harder to spot, because a stale figure still looks like a figure.
:::


## `patchwork`: several panels, one figure {.smaller}

```r
library(patchwork)

p_box  <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot()
p_scat <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) + geom_point()
p_time <- ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, colour = arm)) + geom_line()

(p_box | p_scat) / p_time +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.smaller}
`|` side by side · `/` stacked · `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")` labels the
panels **A**, **B**, **C** the way a journal wants them.

Optional extension package: `install.packages("patchwork")` if needed.
:::



## Summary {.smaller}

- Choose a figure from the statistical question and observation unit.
- Base R supports complete figures with drawing commands, annotations, and file devices.
- A ggplot is a specification of mappings, layers, scales, coordinates, facets, and theme.
- Mapping a variable differs from setting a display property.
- Show distributions and uncertainty rather than only summary bars.
- Exported dimensions, labels, accessibility, and reproducibility are part of the figure.
